In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
S1P can stimulate MC to release VEGF-A in mouse MC and VEGF-A, MMP-2 in human MC.
the S1P/SIPR2 axis can promote MC angiogenic potential through VEGF-A upregulation and MMP-2 secretion, which can further promote angiogenesis.
S1PR2 signaling on MC is important in the regulation of VEGF and MMP-2 release, and this is relevant in inflammation and angiogenesis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
S1P is released upon MC activation, binds to S1PR2 on MC, and triggers proangiogenic VEGF-A, MMP-2 release from MC.
S1P can stimulate VEGF-A production and secretion in MC, a process which is mediated through S1PR2 and is more pronounced in human compared to mouse MC.
S1P can promote VEGF-A/MMP-2 secretion from MC through S1PR2, and this may be a potential target for antiangiogenic therapies.
The main takeaway from our work is that
S1P ligation on MC triggers VEGF-A/MMP-2 release, which can promote vascularization and angiogenesis in the microenvironment of MC.
S1P and S1PR2 can regulate VEGF-A expression in mouse and human MC, and MMP-2 in human MC, suggesting that the S1P/SPIR2 axis can promote angiogenesis.
S1PR2-mediated MC stimulation may contribute to the development of angiogenesis, a hallmark of inflammatory disease.
